guide.summary: This unit covers wave properties, sound, standing waves on strings and in pipes, intensity, the Doppler effect, and wave optics: double-slit and grating interference, single-slit diffraction, and thin-film interference. Proportional reasoning about wavelength, slit spacing, and screen distance is central.

sections.heading: Waves and sound
sections.body: Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to propagation (light, waves on strings); longitudinal waves oscillate parallel (sound). Wave speed v = fλ depends on the medium; frequency is set by the source. Sound intensity from a point source decreases as 1/r² (I = P/4πr²). Loudness relates to amplitude; pitch to frequency. Doppler effect: when source and observer approach, observed frequency increases; when they separate, it decreases. Beats occur when two close frequencies interfere: f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|.

sections.heading: Standing waves
sections.body: Standing waves form from interference of waves traveling in opposite directions, with nodes (no displacement) and antinodes (maximum displacement). Strings fixed at both ends and pipes open at both ends: λ_n = 2L/n, f_n = nv/2L (all harmonics). Pipes closed at one end: λ_n = 4L/n with only odd n: f = nv/4L, n = 1, 3, 5…; the fundamental of a closed pipe is half that of an open pipe of the same length.

sections.heading: Interference and diffraction
sections.body: Superposition: waves add; constructive interference occurs when path difference = mλ, destructive when path difference = (m + ½)λ. Double slit: bright fringes at d sin θ = mλ; for small angles, fringe spacing Δy = λL/d. Increasing λ or L spreads fringes; increasing d compresses them. Diffraction gratings (many slits) produce sharper, more widely spaced bright maxima using the same equation. Single-slit diffraction produces a wide central maximum; narrower slits spread light more. Diffraction is significant when the opening is comparable to the wavelength.

sections.heading: Thin films
sections.body: Light reflecting from the top and bottom of a thin film interferes. A reflection from a medium of higher index causes a half-wavelength phase shift; from lower index, none. With one phase shift (e.g., soap film in air), constructive reflection occurs when 2nt = (m + ½)λ and destructive when 2nt = mλ; with zero or two shifts, the conditions swap. Anti-reflective coatings use destructive interference.

keyTakeaways: v = fλ; frequency fixed by source.
Open/string: f_n = nv/2L; closed: odd n, f_n = nv/4L.
Double slit: d sin θ = mλ; Δy = λL/d.
Path difference mλ → constructive; (m + ½)λ → destructive.
Thin films: count phase shifts before applying conditions.
commonMistakes: Changing frequency instead of wavelength when a wave enters a new medium.
Including even harmonics for closed pipes.
Thinking larger slit spacing spreads fringes.
Ignoring the reflection phase shift in thin films.
Using wavelength in air rather than in the film for thin-film calculations (use 2nt).
examTips: Interference questions: state the path difference condition, then solve.
Standing wave questions: sketch nodes and antinodes to find λ in terms of L.
Proportional reasoning: how does Δy change if λ doubles and d halves? (×4)
Doppler questions are qualitative: higher pitch when approaching.
guide.cramSheet:
**Waves:** v = fλ · transverse vs longitudinal · I ∝ 1/r² · beats |f₁ − f₂|

**Doppler:** approach ↑f · recede ↓f

**Standing:** string/open λ = 2L/n · closed λ = 4L/n (odd n)

**Interference:** Δpath = mλ bright · (m + ½)λ dark

**Double slit:** d sin θ = mλ · Δy = λL/d

**Grating:** same equation, sharper maxima

**Thin film:** phase shift at higher n · one shift: 2nt = (m + ½)λ bright

practice.prompt: Monochromatic light of wavelength λ passes through two narrow slits separated by distance d and forms an interference pattern on a screen a distance L away (L ≫ d).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) the pattern on the screen and label the central maximum and the first-order bright fringes on each side.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Starting from the condition for constructive interference, derive an expression for the distance y₁ from the central maximum to the first-order bright fringe in terms of λ, L, and d. State any approximation.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) a graph of y₁ as a function of slit separation d, for fixed λ and L.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain how the shape of your graph in (C) is consistent with your expression in (B) and with what happens to the pattern in (A) as the slits are moved closer together.

rubric.description: Alternating bright and dark fringes, evenly spaced.
Central maximum at center; first-order bright fringes symmetric on either side.
Path difference d sin θ = mλ, with m = 1.
Small angle: sin θ ≈ tan θ.
Becomes very large as d → 0 and approaches zero as d grows (concave up, not linear).
Hyperbolic shape; doubling d halves y₁.
d is in the denominator, so y₁ ∝ 1/d.
Moving slits closer together spreads the fringes apart on the screen.
Explicitly connects graph, expression, and pattern.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. The screen shows a series of evenly spaced bright fringes separated by dark fringes. The brightest fringe is at the center (the central maximum). The first-order bright fringes appear one fringe spacing to each side of center.

B. For constructive interference, the path difference between waves from the two slits must be a whole number of wavelengths: d sin θ = mλ. For the first-order fringe, m = 1, so sin θ = λ/d. From the geometry, tan θ = y₁/L. Because L ≫ d, the angle is small, so sin θ ≈ tan θ. Therefore y₁/L = λ/d, giving y₁ = λL/d.

C. The graph of y₁ vs. d is a decreasing, concave-up curve: y₁ is very large for small d and approaches zero for large d. Doubling d halves y₁.

D. In y₁ = λL/d, the slit separation is in the denominator, so y₁ is inversely proportional to d, which produces the hyperbola-shaped graph. If the slits are moved closer together (smaller d), y₁ increases, so the bright fringes in the pattern spread farther apart on the screen, consistent with both the graph and the expression.
